articles.title_orig: Bomb threats hit multiple flights in Europe for a second time in a week
articles.title_zh: Bomb threats hit multiple flights in Europe for a second time in a week
articles.content_orig:
Flights across Europe were targeted by "hoax" bomb threats on Thursday for the second time this week, disrupting air travel across London, Dublin, and Helsinki, among others.
At least 27 different flights were impacted, according to Reuters , with some forced to land unexpectedly and others escorted by fighter jets.
Aer Lingus, Finnair , Wizz Air and Polish airline LOT confirmed to CNBC that some of their flights were affected.
It comes after seven passenger planes across Europe, two departing from the U.K., were targeted by suspected bomb threats on Tuesday and were described as "malicious hoax threats" by the U.K. government.
Finnair said two of its flights — one from Helsinki to Rome with 144 passengers and 7 crew members and another from Helsinki to Vienna with 177 passengers and six crew members — received "unfounded or hoax" bomb threats on Thursday, with both flights landing safely and customers disembarking the aircraft.
Local authorities in Rome and Vienna inspected the two flights and didn't find anything out of the ordinary.
"Unfortunately, air traffic is sometimes subject to threats, as we have seen this week, when other airlines in Europe have also faced hoax bomb threats," Finnair said in a statement. "Threats are almost always unfounded."
Hungarian budget carrier Wizz Air confirmed to CNBC that its flight from Milan's Malpensa Airport to Bucharest's Otopeni Airport, as well as another flight to Warsaw, were subject to bomb threats on Thursday.
The flight to Bucharest was approaching its final destination and landed safely when the threat was reported at Otopeni, with security checks subsequently clearing the aircraft. Wizz Air's Warsaw flight was diverted.
"This incident comes amid a series of similar bomb threats affecting several airlines across Europe in recent days," Wizz Air told CNBC. "Wizz Air is not the only airline targeted, with other carriers also experiencing threats resulting in flight diversions and security checks."
Irish airline Aer Lingus diverted its Dublin to Rome flight to Normandy on Thursday morning, while Polish airline LOT said two of its flights from Warsaw received security threats. Both were cleared following security inspections, the airlines told CNBC.
Air France's CEO Ben Smith said none of its flights were affected, but the coordinated threats are unprecedented. "It's unfortunate, and we hope it won't give consumers any reason to slow down or reduce their travel plans."
U.S. Transport Secretary Sean Duffy told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Thursday that the incidents appeared to be "false attacks."
He added: "We take safety very seriously, which is why, if you see any issue in the airspace or threats in the airspace, we shut it down...and so, with all of our assets in the U.S. government and our partners over in Europe, we are tracking this together and working together to make sure the American airspace, the American traveler, is safe."
European Union Commissioner for Sustainable Transport and Tourism, Apostolos Tzitzikostas cautioned it is "too early to draw conclusions on whether the reported incidents are linked," in a post on X . "The EU-level information-sharing mechanism has been activated related to aviation security."

articles.title_orig: ‘I worry people will forget Hong Kong’: Joshua Wong laments city’s fate from inside maximum security prison
articles.title_zh: ‘I worry people will forget Hong Kong’: Joshua Wong laments city’s fate from inside maximum security prison
articles.content_orig:
Wong, 30, in prison since 2020, is only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under national security law
Exclusive: Joshua Wong laments city’s fate from inside maximum security prison
The Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong has been sentenced to 10 years in prison after earlier pleading guilty to “foreign collusion”, his second conviction under a national security law critics say has been used to silence political opposition in the city.
Wong, who rose to prominence as the teenage face of Hong Kong’s 2014 pro-democracy demonstrations, submitted his guilty plea in September. He had been accused of working with the exiled Hong Kong activist Nathan Law to urge foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades or other hostile measures against China.
In his ruling on Thursday, the high ​court judge William Tam ‌described Wong’s actions as “grave in nature”.
He said Wong had visited the US to seek foreign interference before the national security law’s introduction in 2020, and continued to share posts on social media by Law calling for sanctions after it was enacted.
Wong’s role was to “supply his underground support” and “arouse the attention of foreign countries to bolster the cause”, the judge said. He described Wong’s actions as part of a “scheme” to collude with foreign governments.
Tam said Wong’s sentence would run concurrently with the remaining term of his previous national security offence.
After the ruling, Law said in a statement: “It’s incredibly sad to see my friend Joshua Wong suffer another sentencing over his peaceful advocacy work for Hong Kong’s democracy. The signal the sentencing sent to the world is that [China] is determined to quash any hopes for freedom and democracy on its soil.”
Amnesty International’s deputy regional director, Sarah Brooks, said: “Today’s sentence is another grim reminder of how Hong Kong’s national security law has become a tool to punish dissent rather than to genuinely protect national security.”
Wong wore a dark blue shirt and thick rimmed spectacles in court, and nodded and bowed as supporters waved. Dozens of people had waited in line outside the court building for the hearing, amid a heavy police presence. A group of international diplomats was also present for the sentencing.
The former student leader is already serving a prison term of four years and eight months, imposed in November 2024, for conspiracy to commit subversion for his role in an unofficial primary election. He has spent nearly six years in detention and had been due to be released in January 2027.
The US consulate in Hong Kong said in a statement that it “strongly condemns” the additional sentence and called for Wong’s immediate release. “Wong has been unjustly imprisoned since December 2020, demonstrating that Beijing will go to extraordinary lengths to silence those who advocate for fundamental freedoms in Hong Kong,” a consular spokesperson said.
Shortly afterwards, China warned against “irresponsible” remarks on Hong Kong’s judicial affairs. “Relevant parties should earnestly respect China’s sovereignty, respect Hong Kong’s legal system, stop making irresponsible remarks regarding the trial of … judicial cases,” the foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, told reporters.
Wong, 30, gained international attention during the 2014 Umbrella protests , which paralysed the city’s financial centre and galvanised a generation of young people. In October 2014, he appeared on the cover of Time magazine under the headline: “The face of protest.”
When protests erupted in 2019 over a proposed extradition bill, Wong was serving a prison sentence for his role in the 2014 demonstrations. He was released at the height of the protests and immediately took to the streets.
The following year, Beijing introduced a sweeping national security law it said was needed to restore stability to the former British colony, but critics say has been used to target political opposition, dissolve civil society groups and silence independent media.
Wong is the only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under the law.

articles.title_zh: Pakistan takes the One China policy into its airspace
articles.content_orig:
Countries have restricted Taiwanese flights on political grounds (Lin Yen Ting/Office of the Taiwan President)
A brief airspace restriction reveals how far Pakistan will go to reassure Beijing over Taiwan.

Pakistan takes the One China policy into its airspace
Reports that Pakistan had last month barred two Taiwanese airlines, its state carrier China Airlines and private carrier EVA Air, from transiting through its airspace raised questions about Islamabad’s interpretation of the One China policy and the extent of Beijing’s influence over its decisions. Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said (Opens in new window) , “The aviation division follows the One China policy, only mainland China is allowed.” The move was all the more unusual given that even China does not impose such restrictions on Taiwanese commercial airlines.
The ban was abruptly reversed, with both airlines granted access to Pakistani airspace until 27 March 2027. This is only a temporary arrangement, however, and no explanation has been given about what happens after the deadline.
The move was all the more unusual given that even China does not impose such restrictions on Taiwanese commercial airlines.
Pakistan and Taiwan have few substantive ties. Islamabad strictly adheres to the One China policy and maintains an “ironclad friendship” with China. Pakistan’s limited links with Taiwan include just over 900 Pakistani nationals (Opens in new window) living there, including students, restaurant owners and other professionals. There is no representative office, nor has there ever been one. There are also no direct flights between the two sides. The only air connection between South Asia and Taiwan is the Taipei–Delhi route (Opens in new window) , which is scheduled to resume on 1 December.
The ban goes beyond what Pakistan’s adherence to the One China policy would normally require. Islamabad is among its strongest adherents, regularly reaffirming (Opens in new window) its commitment and unconditionally supporting China’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, including its position on Taiwan. At the risk of simplifying a complex issue, a strict adherence, like that of Pakistan’s, generally means opposing Taiwan’s independence, accepting Beijing’s claim that Taiwan is part of China, and not maintaining official ties with Taipei. However, countries interpret (Opens in new window) the policy differently. Some that adhere to it still maintain trade ties and unofficial offices in Taiwan. The policy does not entail that countries deny Taiwanese commercial airlines permission to transit through their airspace. Such permission is a matter of civil aviation arrangements.
Countries have restricted Taiwanese flights on political grounds. In April this year, Seychelles, Mauritius and Madagascar withdrew overflight permissions (Opens in new window) for Taiwan’s incumbent President Lai Ching-te’s planned trip to Eswatini, Taiwan’s only remaining diplomatic ally in Africa. But, restricting a presidential flight is an entirely different issue from denying overflight rights to commercial airlines.
China Airlines flight from Taipei, 19 October 2026 (cifraser1/Flickr)
So, what could have prompted the decision? Was it an extension of China’s grey-zone activities (Opens in new window) , or a show of loyalty arising from the China-Pakistan all-weather friendship?
There are two possible explanations for Pakistan’s decision. The first is that China asked Pakistan to impose the ban to reinforce the One China policy, discourage international engagement with Taiwan and demonstrate Beijing’s influence over its partners. Pakistan remains one of China’s most reliable supporters of its position on Taiwan.
The second possibility is that Pakistan imposed the ban on its own initiative to show its loyalty to China, particularly at a time when it is seeking closer ties with the United States. The Mecca Pact may have added to Islamabad’s incentive to reassure Beijing. Meanwhile, the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor, a flagship component of the Belt and Road Initiative, has become a security liability (Opens in new window) rather than a strategic and economic asset for Beijing. Against this backdrop, the ban may have been a token gesture to show that Pakistan’s efforts to move closer to Washington have not come at the expense of its relationship with China. Although overflight permissions have since been restored, at least for the time being, the message to Beijing is already delivered.
Pakistani airspace is useful for Taiwanese flights travelling to Middle East and Europe. If there is a renewed ban after the March 2027 deadline, it may not have major long-term implications for Taiwan, but rerouting would add to the duration and cost of operating these routes. The episode is also a reminder that Pakistan wants to remain useful to China and is willing to demonstrate that usefulness through decisions affecting Taiwan.
The greater concern is whether this sets a precedent. China could use similar pressure to influence other countries that are close to Beijing and strongly adhere to the One China policy, creating problems for Taiwanese airlines, particularly given Taipei’s lack of representation in the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO). Restrictions on commercial aviation can potentially become another means of exerting pressure on Taiwan.
The decision is further evidence of China’s already formidable influence over Pakistan and Islamabad’s willingness to go further in demonstrating its loyalty to Beijing. But it does little for Pakistan. Applying the One China policy to commercial aviation imposes a restriction with little benefit beyond political signalling. More problematic is Pakistan’s readiness to extend its interpretation of the policy into areas not traditionally associated with it, adding new dimensions to and further complicating an already complex issue.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine continues strikes on Russian refineries in lead-up to White House meeting
articles.title_zh: Ukraine continues strikes on Russian refineries in lead-up to White House meeting
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine has inflicted a dual strike on Vladimir Putin's Russia, hitting an oil refinery and logistics center within hours using long-range drones.
Reports said the attacks struck Russia's third-largest oil refinery and a Wildberries logistics hub in the western Ryazan region, setting both ablaze.
Wildberries processes almost a million orders a day and has been described as a Russian version of Amazon.
"Fires broke out at industrial facilities in Ryazan. Power lines were damaged, causing electricity disruptions in parts of the city," regional Governor Pavel Malkov said .
Pictures posted on social media showed large fires at the Ryazan refinery, which can process 17 million metric tons of crude oil a year. Russian independent media outlet Astra said pictures also showed fires at the Wilberries hub, which covers 173,000 square meters.
Malkov said one person was injured in the strikes, and falling drone debris also caused damage.
It's the latest in a wave of Ukrainian strikes on Russian infrastructure that are causing mounting military and domestic woes for the Kremlin.
Earlier in the week, Ukraine said the success of its operation means Russia is being forced to use substandard imported jet fuel for its military planes, causing one to blow up.
On the frontline in Ukraine, the attacks are hampering Russia's campaign, which has failed to make significant advances for months amid fuel shortages and heavy manpower losses.
And Russian civilians are also feeling the bite, with inflation spiking and long queues at gas stations throughout the country.
Ukraine says it has knocked out half of Russia's refining capacity this year . It's launched more than 300 strikes, more than two dozen of which have hit refineries, using sophisticated long-range drones.
It's forced Russia, the world's third-largest oil producer, to start importing fuel from abroad and halt aviation fuel exports.
The Ryazan facility was also successfully hit on October 15, shutting down one of its processing hubs.
President Donald Trump, before the midterms, attempted to pin the blame on rising U.S. fuel prices caused by his war with Iran on Ukraine's strikes, and pressured Kyiv to call them off.
Ukraine temporarily halted them but has since has launched a new series of attacks, successfully hitting refineries in Kstovo, Yaroslavl, and the Samara region this week alone.
Russia has responded with brutal missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian civilian targets and infrastructure.

articles.title_zh: Record share of first-time homebuyers paying in cash as Great Wealth Transfer picks up steam
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
The Great Wealth Transfer is starting to impact the housing market.
A record share of first-time homebuyers are paying for their properties in cash, a sign that more buyers are likely using money they inherited from older generations to help fund their purchases.
Last year, 1 in 10 first-time buyers did an all-cash transaction, according to a new report from the National Association of Realtors, the fourth straight year with an increase, and the largest share since the trade group began collecting data on those transactions in 2003. Among first-time all-cash buyers, 28% reported using an inheritance to help fund their deal, compared with just 9% of first-time buyers who financed.
As home prices hover near all-time highs and mortgage rates stay north of 7% , pricing out many prospective buyers, some portion of those buyers may simply be waiting for an inheritance or other significant help from wealthy baby boomers or members of the Silent Generation.
"It is critical when analyzing first-time buyers to understand there is a growing divide among those who are saving independently and priced out of homeownership, versus those who are waiting on the sidelines but then given a generational transfer of wealth," the report said.
Buyers reliant on wealth transfers look different from those who finance and use their own savings. As modern life expectancy increases, delaying inheritances, first-time all-cash buyers are typically deep into middle age. The median first-time buyer paying all cash is 54 years old, according to the report, significantly older than the median age of 38 for first-time buyers financing their homes.
Claire Boston is a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance covering housing, mortgages, and home insurance.

articles.title_orig: How Melania Trump Became a Dark Horse Diplomat on Ukraine
articles.title_zh: How Melania Trump Became a Dark Horse Diplomat on Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Olha has one word to describe what life has been like in the front-line city of Oleshky over the past few years: "Horror".
Disembarking alongside her from a coach in the Ukrainian region of Chernihiv with their immediate family and dog, her husband Viacheslav put it this way: "We came back from hell."
The couple were among hundreds of residents evacuated from the Russian-occupied city who crossed into northern Ukraine via Belarus on Saturday, many reuniting with loved ones they had not seen for years.
Oleshky, seized by Russia during the first few days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022, is trapped on one side by the Dnipro River and on the other side by Russian forces.
Olha and Viacheslav had lived there with their son and daughter, both in their 30s. Even as the shelling around them intensified, they feared that trying to escape could be even more dangerous, with routes mined and subject to drone attack.
As supplies dwindled, the couple said they made an attempt to find food by crossing through minefields earlier this month. "People were stepping on mines, dying and being maimed, all just to survive," Olha told the BBC.
Those who were too afraid to go out in the city had resorted to cooking garden weeds to survive.
"We saw that the situation wasn't getting any better, so we realised we had to get out," Olha said.
That opportunity came earlier this week when a humanitarian ceasefire, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, took effect in the Kherson region, providing the first few days of peace in the area for four years and allowing Oleshky residents to evacuate.
Up to 6,000 people, including 200 children, were believed to still be living in Oleshky and its surrounding areas, with 1,700 in the city itself.
Residents had a four-hour window on Friday to leave, with a convoy of 25 buses brought in for up to 750 evacuees, along with ambulances for people with limited mobility.
After travelling through Russian-occupied territory to southern Russia, then flying to Belarus, evacuees arrived on buses to a military facility in Chernihiv on Saturday.
On the tarmac, where evacuees were processed before travelling onwards, some elderly residents were so weak they had to be carried on stretchers.
For many, there were emotional reunions.
As Mykhailo Palii arrived, his daughters Dasha and Anya, who thought they might never see him again, sprinted across the tarmac screaming and crying.
After an emotional embrace, Palii described a glimpse of life in Oleshky, although he said he had, until then, kept many of the details from his family.
"A hole was blown into the bathroom," he said. "There were drone attacks and missile strikes. It happened, but I didn't tell them about it because I knew they would worry."
Tetiana and Volodymyr, a couple carrying a cat when they arrived in Chernihiv, said their entire home was burned down three years ago, and they had been living in the abandoned house of a neighbour since.
For them, leaving as soon as it was safe to do so was an easy decision. "There's nothing for us to regret leaving. We don't have relatives there. Our children are married and don't live with us in the city," said Tetiana.
But those who managed to escape also worry about those left behind. "There are still a lot of people left there, living under those conditions," said Olha.
Now that the evacuees have left Oleshky, they will also face a new challenge - working out where to go next and how to rebuild their lives.
Palii said he would look for a job so he can provide for his family: "There's no job I can't handle. Digging, hoeing, planting, building. I can even do demolition work."
Olha said she and her family have no relatives elsewhere in Ukraine, and they will stay with some acquaintances for an extended period while they get back on their feet.
"If we managed to survive in hell, we'll survive here too."

articles.title_orig: Nvidia Stock Is Below $200. What History Suggests Is the Floor.
articles.title_zh: Nvidia Stock Is Below $200. What History Suggests Is the Floor.
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
For all the interviews Nvidia ( NVDA ) CEO Jensen Huang has been doing over the past six months, banging the drum for a powerful AI future in the process (powered by his chips, naturally), you would think shares of the AI chip darling would be trading on peak valuation multiples.
And you would be wrong. It couldn't be further from the truth, especially in the wake of a fresh tech stock rout to kick off the fall.
Nvidia shares trade on a mere forward PE ratio of 12.9 times, per Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace data. For perspective on how shocking this is, the S&P 500, filled with far slower earnings growers than Nvidia, trades on a forward PE ratio of 18.7 times.
What's more, Nvidia's stock trades on a paltry 0.27 times price to earnings growth ratio, better known as the PEG ratio. And for a dose of perspective here, Coca-Cola ( KO ) shares trade at a PEG ratio of 2.57 times. While Coca-Cola has been doing well, it's not an expected growth juggernaut in the same vein as Nvidia.
The stock is down 11% in the past month.
Tech stocks like Nvidia aren't getting shredded for any old reason.
It's actually very fundamental.
First, free cash flow is drying up at Big Tech leaders such as Alphabet, Meta and Amazon, and capex is going up dramatically. Investors are questioning whether this ratio is totally out of whack given more realistic growth projections around AI.
Second, there is concern these hyperscalers will have to cut back on capex in 2027 to appease nervous investors. That could mean fewer than expected AI chip orders from Nvidia.
The AI trade saw a serious slamming on Friday, with more than $1 trillion in market value wiped away as investors fretted about the weakening cash flow profiles of Big Tech. Nvidia's stock finished the session down 4.22%.
"The AI narrative is cracking as profitability concerns intensify," warmed Miller Tabak chief markets strategist Matt Maley.

articles.title_orig: The US Midterm Elections: Views From China - The Diplomat
articles.title_zh: The US Midterm Elections: Views From China - The Diplomat
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. midterm elections on November 3 were closely watched around the world as a way to gauge public support for the polarizing administration of Donald Trump. The verdict is in: the opposition Democratic Party won big, taking control of both houses of Congress with majorities Democrats haven’t enjoyed in years. Several states elected Democratic senators and governors for the first time in decades – in some cases, nearly a century .
Officially, of course, China won’t comment on the results of the election. That, as Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters on November 4, is “a domestic affair” of the United States. “China stands ready to continue working with the U.S. to uphold and deliver on the important common understandings reached by the two heads of state,” Mao said.
In a speech delivered on election day, Xie Feng, China’s ambassador to the United States, said , “A confident and composed China is committed to the steady, sound, and sustainable development of China-U.S. relations… China’s policy toward the United States remains consistent and stable.”
The first news readouts from Xinhua, China’s state news agency, were also terse, although the points of information they chose to include were telling. In one early article , for example, Xinhua did not mention the historic nature of Democratic Party wins, but instead quoted Trump’s social media post that “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” The short, three-paragraph report also devoted the entire last paragraph to comments from a White House official, who predicted U.S. voters “will suffer from severe buyer’s remorse.”
Xinhua published a much longer analysis on November 4, highlighting four “unexpected” outcomes. This article delved into the massive scale of the Democratic victory, from the size of its new House majority to the flipping of Senate seats in traditionally safe Republican states like Texas, Iowa, Kansas, and South Carolina.
Rather than offering perspectives from Chinese analysts, Xinhua’s article extensively cited U.S. media, including this quote from the Wall Street Journal : “Rarely in American politics has a president traded away so much political support so quickly. The losses that Republicans suffered on Tuesday marked one of the most decisive repudiations of a president in modern history.”
Chinese state media had much less to say about the causes of the Republican defeat – again, Beijing’s official line being that this is an “internal affair” of the United States. However, Xinhua did cite the general thesis by U.S. analysts that economic dissatisfaction amid rising prices was the primary culprit. And those rising prices were exacerbated by the Trump administration’s decision to strike Iran. Xinhua published a whole article covering Vice President J.D. Vance’s post-election verdict that the war on Iran had cost the Republicans control of Congress.
One Xinhua report cited Iran’s Speaker of Parliament Mohammad Ghalibaf, who posted on X : “Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message.”
“What the Chinese public is most concerned about … is the impact of the U.S. midterm election results on the Iran war and Ukraine war,” Mu Chunshan, an independent political analysts based in Beijing, told The Diplomat via email. “They are less focused on the impact on China-U.S. relations. This is because Trump has consistently shown respect to China.”
If Democrats act to restrain Trump’s military operations in Iran, Mu said, it would be align “with China’s long-standing call for a peaceful resolution of the Iran nuclear issue.” He sees the election results as “conducive to China and other countries pushing for a negotiated resolution of the Iran nuclear issue and Strait [of Hormuz] security issues.”
That said, Chinese analysts are well aware of Congress’ limited control over foreign policy. In an pre-election analysis, South China Morning Post cited Zhao Zhijiang , a research assistant at the Beijing-based independent think tank Anbound, as predicting that “Diplomacy may become even more transactional. U.S. policy towards Russia, Iran, Europe and China could swing rapidly between heavy pressuring and partial bargaining.” In other words, China is bracing for impact as a notoriously mercurial leader feels increased political pressure at home.
Diao Daming, an international relations professor at Renmin University in Beijing, told SCMP Trump might become more “legacy-driven” in his pursuit of foreign policy.  “On the other hand, in areas he believes he can control or achieve results quickly, he may also take some risky actions,” Diao said.
With a Trump-Xi summit looming later this month, China will be one of the first to get a feel for how the midterm defeat impacts Trump’s foreign policy style. China is hosting the APEC Leaders’ Meeting from November 18-19, with Trump expected to attend. Beside yet another summit between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping – the third in 2026 alone – there has been much discussion of other potential sideline meetings, including a possible China-Russia-U.S. trilateral.
China had its own reasons to be skeptical about hosting such a meeting . After the midterm outcomes, which will likely result in increased congressional support for Ukraine, there’s even less reason for Beijing to look positively on the prospects of a Putin-Trump-Xi meeting.
“At the APEC summit, if China, the US and Russia hold a trilateral summit, there is a high probability that the Ukraine war will not be discussed, because the midterm results make it harder for Trump to pressure Ukraine into accepting a ‘land-for-peace’ plan.” Mu said. “For China, discussing this is meaningless. Any peace plan must indeed fully take into account the views of Ukraine and Europe. This should be similar to the views of the new U.S. Congress.”
Also with the APEC summit in mind, Chinese policymakers will want to see if Trump is willing to strike a bargain to secure quick economic gains, given U.S. voter anger over the cost of living. There is also hope that a Democratic Congress would do more to push back on Trump’s use of tariffs – a tool that typically belongs to the legislative branch, not the executive, under the U.S. system of government.
“If the Democrats can restrain Trump’s impulses to China and other countries in the areas of tariffs and trade, that would be better for China-U.S. relations,” Mu said.
But few in China expect a Democratic-majority Congress to look too much different. “Structural contradictions exist in China-U.S. relations, and both the two parties share negative views on China, for example on national security or high-tech competition,” Mu noted. “These will not change in any particular way due to the outcome of the midterms.”
More broadly, Chinese analysts largely took the U.S. election results as evidence for already-held assumptions about a crumbling U.S. political system. Xinhua’s own original reporting , including on-the-street interviews with voters, portrayed a sense of pessimism and despair. Nearly all the quotes were from voters who expressed doubt that anything would change, regardless of who is in power. One sample: “I have no confidence in any politician, and I don’t think they will focus on what is right for us.”
That was a far cry from the palpable sense of optimism emanating from the Democratic Party as the election results rolled in. But it does fit nearly with China’s preferred thesis that the United States is locked into an irreversible decline.
And whatever Beijing may say about the election being the United States’ “domestic affair,” it will not be lost on Chinese leaders that an unpopular war far from home, and its economic consequences, resulted in severe political punishment for the ruling party. That will factor in to China’s ongoing calculations about what the Iran-U.S. war might imply about Americans’ appetite for intervention in a Taiwan crisis.

The slump on Wall Street has rippled across to the London stock market too.
The FTSE 100 share index has closed for the night, down 46 points or 0.4% at 10,782 points.
Earlier this morning the ‘Footsie’ had been up over 100 points.
Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, says:
double quotation mark ‘Fresh panic over the AI trade has hit Wall Street hard, with a steep sell-off on the Nasdaq, and the S&P 500 sending shockwaves rippling to other markets. Fears that the vast sums poured into AI infrastructure may not deliver the returns investors have been banking on are now colliding with the prospect of a sharp slowdown in data centre construction. Chip stocks have been the hardest hit with AMD down 13%, Nvidia falling around 7% and Intel another 5.5%.
The contagion is spreading - the FTSE 100, which had been on the front foot and is far less exposed to big tech, has now erased its earlier gains and turned negative. Even a tech-lite index with defensive appeal hasn’t been able to shrug off this big case of the jitters.
Back on Wall Street, the Dow Jones industrial average (DJIA) has slumped by 2.5%, or 1,346 points, as shares retreat sharply.
Both the S&P 500 share index and the tech-focused Nasdaq has hit their lowest levels since late July, and on track for their biggest one-day drop in five months.
Chip giant Nvidia is leading the selloff on the DJIA , down 8%, followed by Goldman Sachs which has dropped by 6.5%.
A December hike in UK interest rates is now “on the table”, argues consultancy Oxford Economics , following today’s rise.
Oxford Economics believes that December’s Monetary Policy Committee meeting “looks like a coin flip”, with oil and natural gas prices set to be the decisive factor.
Their chief UK economist Andrew Goodwin reckons the committee’s messaging was more hawkish than before.
double quotation mark “Higher energy futures prices and more evidence of domestic resilience both increase the risk of second-round effects emerging.
The degree of inflationary pressure already in the system means another hike in December or February is likely.”
America’s technology share index, the Nasdaq Composite, has fallen into correction territory.
The Nasdaq Composite is down 4% today, as tech stocks drop sharply, and is now more than 10% below its record closing high.
Oil and gas aren’t the only volatile elements in the markets today, following the events of the last 48 hours.
Over on Wall Street, Elon Musk’s businesses are being hit in the aftermath of the midterm election results.
Shares in Tesla and SpaceX are both down around 9% in early trading, adding to losses yesterday that wiped billions of dollars off both company’s valuation.
The midterms have been something of a disaster for Musk.
He contributed at least $446m to Republican-aligned Super Pacs and groups over the course of the elections, specifically targeting several key Senate races in an effort to help the Trump administration retain Republican control of Congress – and then watched the Democrats rack up a series of election wins.
Voters across the US also voted for bans or restrictions on datacentre development, in a backlash against AI.
Several economists are arguing that today’s rise in UK interest rates is not the start of a long cycle of rate hikes.
Sanjay Raja , Deutsche Bank’s chief UK economist, says today’s move is an “insurance policy” against the danger ofsecond-round effects (a wage-price spiral), arguing:
double quotation mark Today’s hike merely adds a dose of policy restriction to an already restrictive policy stance. Moreover, with financial conditions having tightened materially since March, the case to go much further isn’t as strong as it may have been in the Bank’s previous hiking cycle back in 2022.
With signs of second-round effects remaining minimal at this juncture, we retain our view for one more hike with Bank Rate peaking at 4.25%. And perhaps the bigger question from today’s decision is whether the next hike comes in December or February. There is a clear risk that the MPC could go earlier – this will be something to watch in the coming weeks and will likely be determined by forthcoming inflation outturns as well as developments in the Middle East (with the last 48 hours delivering some good news on energy price expectations).
Modupe Adegbembo, economist at investment bank Jefferies , believes another hike is likely, but not a foregone conclusion, telling clients:
double quotation mark February is our base case, but the MPC looks willing to pause if the backdrop improves materially.
A resolution to the conflict or a further meaningful stabilisation in energy prices would reduce the need for another move, particularly if second-round effects remain limited. So we think the bias is towards another hike in February, but it remains conditional on the energy shock and evidence of persistence.
Daniel Siluk , head of global short duration & liquidity at Janus Henderson Investors , is also cautious about interpreting today’s decision as the beginning of a prolonged hiking cycle.
double quotation mark The energy shock is lifting headline inflation, but there remains relatively limited evidence that it is becoming embedded in broader wages and prices. At the same time, higher energy bills, elevated mortgage rates and tighter financial conditions are increasingly weighing on household purchasing power and should ultimately slow demand. Andrew Bailey was careful to stress that today’s move should not be viewed as the first in a sequence of increases. Our view is that the Bank is effectively buying some insurance against second-round inflation effects and protecting its inflation-fighting credibility.
One further increase looks increasingly plausible, but the bigger question for markets is whether the considerably longer tightening cycle currently reflected in the curve will ultimately be delivered.
That was the end of the Bank’s press conference – here’s our news story about the interest rate hike:
Q: You say the best thing that can happen is, is to resolve the conflict in the Middle East. Given the events of the last 48 hours, would you make that plea directly to US President Donald Trump or the Republican Party for the sake of the UK economy or global economy? (asks Hannah Brenton of Politico).
Andrew Bailey replies that prime minister Andy Burnham put this pont very clearly in the last 24 hours, speaking at the Commonwealth summit [where the PM said the midterm election results are an “opportunity” to focus on ending the Iran war].
Bailey says he supports Burnham on this issue, explaining:
double quotation mark I mean, he also made the same point about Russia’s illegal invasion of Ukraine.

articles.title_orig: Meloni urges ‘disorganized’ EU to speak with one voice on Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Meloni urges ‘disorganized’ EU to speak with one voice on Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
ROME — The EU is giving the impression of being “all over the place” when it comes to Ukraine, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni told European Council President António Costa.
In a letter seen by POLITICO, Meloni said that discussing how the EU can speak with one voice on Ukraine should be added to the agenda of an informal leaders’ meeting in Dublin next week, adding that the issue “can no longer be postponed.”
Meloni pointed out the various formats that have been used to discuss Ukraine, including meetings in Miami and Oslo, and upcoming talks scheduled by the Coalition of the Willing and the European Political Community, plus the phone call that Finland’s Alexander Stubb and Norway’s Jonas Gahr Støre made to Russia’s Vladimir Putin. She said the multiple forums were “undermining our credibility in handling one of the most complicated issues our nations are facing.”
While the EU has repeatedly insisted it gets a “seat at the table” at Ukraine peace talks, to  safeguard the region’s interests and bolster Kyiv’s ability to resist a lopsided deal, the bloc has yet to agree on a single leader or institution to spearhead negotiations.
“I’m convinced that we all realize how, by projecting the image of a Europe that’s all over the place, we’re doing nothing but serving the interests of those who want this war to continue,” the Italian prime minister wrote. “And I think this is unacceptable, given that human lives and the future of our security are at stake.”
“Proceeding in a disorganized manner, with initiatives that chase one another and overlap, will not help us — neither with our partners nor with those we must convince to stop this senseless aggression,” she added.
“I am not asking for a seat for Italy in this or that format,” she said.
EU leaders meet in Dublin for an informal European Council on Nov. 13. A meeting of the European Political Community, which involves all EU states plus Ukraine and other allies, takes place the day before.
As the format for talks increasingly coalesces around the E3 — the U.K., France and Germany — alongside the EU, NATO and Ukraine, Italy has found itself sidelined.
Rome was excluded from meetings in Miami in October and Brussels this week, although it did take part in talks in Oslo at the invitation of the Norwegian government. An Italian national security adviser attended a working dinner there, but Italy’s participation came in place of France, rather than as an additional seat at the table.
Over the past year, Italy has emerged as the EU’s most vocal and persistent advocate for appointing a special envoy for Russia-Ukraine peace talks. Meloni first publicly floated the proposal in January, arguing that the bloc needed to “speak with one voice” and engage directly with Moscow.
While other countries, including France, Austria, Czechia and Luxembourg, have also expressed support for the idea, Rome has led the push, with Italian officials repeatedly raising it on the sidelines of EU summits and in discussions among EU ambassadors preparing leaders’ meetings.
Ahead of the latest EU summit in October, Italian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani seized an opportunity during an exchange with reporters at a European People’s Party pre-summit gathering to renew the call for a special envoy.
Asked whether Costa himself should take on the role, Tajani praised him but insisted that the priority was for Europe to have “a spokesperson who can negotiate” and articulate a “univocal position,” warning that otherwise EU foreign policy would appear weak.
Gerardo Fortuna and Elena Giordano contributed reporting. This article has been updated.

articles.content_orig:
Wendy’s rejected a $1.4 billion buyout offer from an activist investor, saying Thursday that the bid was too low
Wendy’s rejected a $1.4 billion buyout offer from an activist investor, saying Thursday that the bid was too low, and it adopted a “poison pill” plan that would make it more difficult to engineer a hostile takeover of the company.
Noted investor Nelson Peltz made an offer last week to buy the chain, which has been struggling with high beef prices and aging stores. Peltz said the fast-food landscape had become increasingly challenging, with consumers under pressure, intensifying competition and persistent inflation, and his offer was the best path forward for shareholders.
But in a conference call with investors Thursday, Wendy's CEO Bob Wright, who joined the company in May from Potbelly, said Wendy's has a turnaround plan in place that is already producing good results.
“We’re confident that we have the right strategy, execution and resources to restore Wendy’s to its full potential and drive meaningful shareholder value,” Wright said.
Shares rose more than 2% Thursday as the company reported a better than expected performance during the third quarter.
Wendy's said in a statement that a committee of independent directors unanimously rejected the offer because it “substantially undervalues” the company.
Wendy's also announced that it has adopted a shareholders' rights plan, a so-called “poison pill,” intended to avert a hostile takeover of the company. The plan, which grants all shareholders except the hostile bidder the right to purchase discounted shares, automatically triggers if a person or group owns 15% or more of Wendy's shares.
Peltz's Trian Fund Management and other partners in the investor group that made the offer to Wendy's hold 16.3% of the company's shares. The plan would stay in place for one year, Wendy's said. Trian didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
Wendy’s has been closing outdated U.S. restaurants so it can focus on its more profitable locations. The company closed 240 restaurants in 2024 and said earlier this year that it planned to shutter up to 358 locations in 2026.
Then, in September, one of the largest U.S. franchisees for Wendy’s filed for bankruptcy protection after the chain tried to terminate its franchise agreement. Michigan-based Meritage Hospitality Group operates 314 Wendy’s restaurants in 15 states.
Wendy’s, which is based in Dublin, Ohio, had 5,969 restaurants in the U.S. and 1,428 outlets in 38 countries at the end of 2025.
Founded in 1969 by Dave Thomas and named after his daughter, Wendy's is known for its square burgers and Frosty desserts. The fast-growing chain introduced the drive-thru window in 1970 and went public in 1976. In the 1980s, as it jockeyed for sales with McDonald’s and Burger King, Wendy’s launched salad bars and ran its iconic “Where’s the beef?” ad campaign.
But as the fast-food market grew even more competitive and rival burger-focused chains like In-N-Out and Five Guys expanded, Wendy’s fell behind. Wendy’s share of U.S. burger chain sales fell from 11.5% in 2019 to 10.4% last year, according to Technomic, a market research company.

articles.content_orig:
Wendy's board of directors on Thursday unanimously rejected a $1.4 billion hostile takeover bid from a group of investment firms, saying the offer undervalues the restaurant chain and is not in the best interest of shareholders.
"The Independent Committee thoroughly evaluated this Proposal and unanimously concluded that it substantially undervalues Wendy's standalone prospects and long-term earnings potential," Art Winkleblack, chairman of the board, said in a statement, while also expressing confidence in CEO Bob Wright.
The takeover bid was led by asset management firm Trian Partners, founded by activist investor Nelson Peltz, along with Flynn Group LP, BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners.
The groups are offering $7.35 per share for Wendy's, whose stock traded at $7.75 before markets opened on Thursday. Wendy's confirmed it received the unsolicited offer last month and said it would create an independent board to review the proposal.
Although it remains profitable, Wendy's has faced slowing revenue growth in recent years, and its stock price has slumped nearly 14% over the last 12 months.
In its latest earnings report on Thursday, Wendy's said that U.S. same-restaurant sales decreased 5.7% in the third quarter, compared with the same period last year. The chain reported $547 million in revenue, down from $549.5 million in the year-ago quarter.
Wendy's is losing traction with customers as inflation and rising beef costs force the burger chain to raise prices, the Associated Press reported last week.
The company has also struggled with operational issues, including staffing, employee training, handling drive-thru orders and marketing, Wright said during a call with Wall Street analysts in August. More broadly, he acknowledged that Wendy's must improve the quality of its food to drive business.
"Wendy's has always been known for quality, fresh, never frozen beef, hamburgers made to order, bacon cooked in our restaurants and fresh produce prepared daily," he said. "But over time, we've drifted away from some of the standards that made Wendy's distinctive. While we've maintained core practices in some areas, we've led cost and efficiency drive decisions that weaken that differentiation."
Other businesses across the fast-food industry are also struggling as inflation weighs on customers' wallets. McDonald's reported on Wednesday that it would offer a new array of affordable options next year to boost sales.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is a lighter, thinner, and all-around better laptop. Oh, and sure, there’s a touchscreen.

I keep forgetting the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display has a touchscreen. I’ve been testing this new laptop, one of the most impressive Apple has ever created, for the better part of a week. I can’t stop noticing some of its other features: the slimmer design, the improved display, the Dynamic Island that somehow catches my eye more than the notch ever did. But I keep forgetting that as I go about my day, I can now reach out and poke the screen.
Come to think of it, that might be exactly what Apple intended. Steve Jobs said touch laptops were a bad idea; some subset of users demanded one anyway. Now the MacBook Pro has one. But not in a way that meaningfully changes the laptop experience. There have been a few times I have found the touchscreen genuinely useful, better or more intuitive than anything I could do with a trackpad or a mouse. But to call this “the touchscreen MacBook Pro” just doesn’t feel right. It’s the latest evolution of Apple’s most powerful laptop — and oh, it happens to have a touchscreen.
Very little about this laptop, or my experience with it, will come as a surprise. That’s a good thing; the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display (which I will just be calling the PROLED Pro from now on, because ugh, the name) comes with a bunch of new upgrades but no new problems, and performs as well as you’d expect from a laptop this expensive. Combine the screen, the body, and the touch, and you have something like a new generation of MacBook Pro. It’s going to be a good one.
The 14-inch PROLED Pro starts at $2,899, and the 16-inch at $3,399. Both come with either an M5 Pro or M5 Max chip, each with two configurations to choose from, plus a bunch of RAM and storage options. It’s a lot of options! (My review unit is a 14-inch model with an M5 Pro chip that has 18 CPU cores and 20 GPU cores, plus 48GB of RAM and 1TB of storage. Total cost: $3,699.) In general, this device runs about a $400 premium over the standard, similarly specced Pro, but spoiler alert: I think it’s worth it, touchscreen or no touchscreen.
If you buy the fully loaded PROLED Pro with the beefiest M5 Max chip, nano-texture glass, 128GB of RAM, and 16TB of storage — at a whopping $14,549 — you are my hero. And I have some questions.
My middle-of-the-road PROLED configuration benchmarks almost exactly in line with other devices running an M5 Pro, such as the most recent Mac Mini . One simple way to think about Apple’s M-series chips is that the cores get faster with every generation, and you get a bunch of additional cores (and faster memory) with the Pro and Max chips. So on a single-core, one-task benchmark, the M5 Pro comes in slightly behind most M6 devices, even much cheaper ones. But as you get to more complex computing tasks, particularly anything involving the GPU, the M5 Pro and Max brute-force their way to better performance.
That means the M5 Pro and Max suit anyone doing heavily graphical work or local AI development. The tests prove these laptops are very fast, which we already knew. They also prove they’re just as fast despite being inside a machine that’s smaller and thinner, which is not always a given. Apple says it redesigned the thermals inside the laptop both to accommodate the new design and to direct heat away from the OLED display, which can degrade or even fail if it gets too hot for too long. The Pro’s fans always seem to turn on before the laptop even gets a little hot — that’s clearly deliberate on Apple’s part.
As for the OLED itself, it’s gorgeous. The slimmer bezels and smaller cutout make it loom even larger and more central in the laptop; it has almost that iPad-like, “magic pane of glass” feel. It’s sharp and contrast-y, gets both very bright (though it only hits peak brightness under very specific conditions) and very dim, and is better even than the very good screens on Apple’s other laptops. Visual professionals will need, and appreciate, the fidelity to P3 and Adobe’s RGB color spaces; the rest of us will probably most notice just how much more dramatic the blacks look as we play games or watch movies. I generally live in dark mode, and it looks even better on this machine.
One theme of Apple’s recent product launches has been how much thinner an OLED display is than an LCD, and what that means for the product as a whole. What it means, mostly, is that the Apple logo can glow again. But also, just as OLED made it possible for the iPad Mini to shrink even more, the PROLED Pro is smaller than its predecessors by an impressive margin. My 14-inch model is a fraction of an inch smaller in every dimension than the standard MacBook Pro , which is always a good thing, but the half-pound weight decrease (more than two-thirds of a pound on the 16-inch model!) is what really impresses me. At 3 pounds on the dot, the 14-inch PROLED Pro is closer in weight to the 15-inch MacBook Air than the 14-inch MacBook Pro. It still feels solid and dense, but I appreciate the slimmer build every time I pick it up or toss it in my backpack.
The only small downside of this new design, at least to my ears, is the speakers. The Pro’s built-in speakers have always been impressive, but I find the new model a bit bass-heavy and roomy. Everything sounds like it’s playing in a large, empty warehouse. Still, these are better speakers than you’ll find in almost any other laptop.
Give it a year or two, and I suspect every model in the MacBook Pro lineup will look like this
Most of the rest of the hardware hasn’t changed. Same three Thunderbolt 5 ports, same HDMI and SD card access, same headphone jack, same keyboard, same trackpad. Even the battery life seems about the same: I get through a pretty heavy workday with a third or more of the battery left. I would always like more ports, especially on a device with this much raw multitasking power, but this appears to be the selection Apple is going with.
Give it a year or two, and I suspect every model in the MacBook Pro lineup will look like this. The OLED display, and the smaller and lighter laptop it enables, are such obvious upgrades that Apple would be silly not to bring them to other devices. Do you need to pay the $400 premium just to get them right now? Probably not. But next time you’re in the market for a MacBook, get one with the new screen and the new look.
So far, we’ve talked about a bunch of things that add up to a better MacBook Pro. If there’s a big new idea about computing in here, it’s the PROLED Pro’s touch support. For the first time ever, the Mac has a touchscreen. The mental model for that touchscreen is very simple: It’s a mouse emulator. When you tap on the screen, the Pro registers it like you’ve clicked the mouse or trackpad. In theory, this should work everywhere; in practice, it works almost everywhere. In a few instances, in particular while playing games, I’ve encountered a button that simply would not respond to touch. And since there’s no touch equivalent to hovering your cursor over a notification or icon, there are a few things you just can’t do with a tap. I can swipe away a notification with a tap, but I can’t make the X appear in the corner to quickly dismiss it.

Bring Khazalite might to armies of Order with Regiments of Renown
For such a stubborn lot, the duardin of the Khazalite Holds work rather well with their Grand Alliance Order allies, and two new Regiments of Renown from their upcoming battletome show you how.
The first, Fjori’s Vengeance, stars the last survivor of Guzanhold and the gaggle of mercenary Fyreslayers he’s gathered to help him wreak ancestral retribution upon those responsible for the magmahold’s fall. As a Grimhold Exile , Fjori is a deadly close combat killer who can normally propel himself to a distant board edge once per game, but now with the Regiment’s new Itinerant Grimmdron rule he can bring the rest of his gang with him too.
Once Per Battle (Army), Deployment Phase
Well used to being outnumbered, Fjori turns the situation to his advantage as he outflanks the foe with his warriors.
Effect: If the Grimhold Exile in this Regiment of Renown has used the ‘Wrathful Wanderer’ ability this battle, remove the other units in this Regiment of Renown from the battlefield and set them up again on the battlefield wholly within 6" of a battlefield edge, wholly within 6" of the Grimhold Exile in this Regiment of Renown and more than 9" from all enemy units. Then, give a unit in this Regiment of Renown 1 grudge mark .
The sudden appearance of tough and dangerous Fyreslayers is a great help to many armies who want to pull enemy troops away from the front line, as it’s pretty hard to ignore someone with the potential to throw out Damage 3 attacks when charging.
Once Per Battle (Army), Deployment Phase
Grimhold Exiles are accustomed to operating alone. They go where they will, and death follows them.
Effect: Remove this unit from the battlefield, then set it up again on the battlefield wholly within 6" of a battlefield edge and more than 9" from all enemy units.
His entourage are equally dangerous and the whole lot can appear from any point near a board edge – great for teaming up with soaring Kharadron Overlords airships or speedy aelven cavalry.
The second Regiment of Renown brings a spot of duardin rune magic to other Order armies courtesy of the eponymous Runewright and his contingent of hardy Khazalite infantry. It’s a sizable force compared to its Grimmdron peers, with 10 Clanshields, 10 Clangunners, the Runewright himself, and an Oathkeeper Cannon to keep enemy heads down.
This Regiment of Renown doubles down on the hardiness of the average duardin and is perfect for less durable armies* who want a hard core to brawl over tricky objectives. The Rune of Stoicism spell is a great little buff that will help your forces stick around a bit longer with Ward 6+, while the Grudgesettlers rule gives them a hefty punch early in the game by starting with an ever-useful grudge token .
The sombre resonance of this rune instils in duardin a stubborn determination.
Declare: Pick the Runewright in this Regiment of Renown to cast this spell, then make a casting roll of 2D6.
Effect: Until the start of your next turn, units in this Regiment of Renown have WARD (6+) while they are wholly within 12" of and visible to this unit.
No matter the grievance, Thengin and his kin are ever ready to mete out retribution.
Effect: Each unit in this Regiment of Renown starts the battle with 1 grudge mark .
If a unit in this Regiment of Renown destroys an enemy unit, you must remove the grudge mark from that friendly unit.
This Regiment of Renown is also a particularly nice way to get some of the lovely new Khazalite Holds miniatures even when you’re not planning to start a full army, as they can be used across the whole spectrum of Grand Alliance Order armies. You get a cannon! We bet the Daughters of Khaine or Idoneth Deepkin would love to have a cannon handy.
Will you be adding a wandering band of hard-headed Khazalites to your army? The Khazalite Holds go on pre-order from Saturday , including Fjori’s Vengeance and the individual units that make up Thengin’s Grudgesettlers.
* Aelves, we’re looking at you here.

articles.title_zh: Israel’s Election Ended With No Clear Winner. These Parties Are Trying to Form a Coalition.
articles.content_orig:
A majority of Israeli lawmakers have backed former military chief Gadi Eisenkot to be given the first chance to form the country's next government, as consultations with President Isaac Herzog continued on Thursday.
A total of 67 of the 120 members of the Knesset endorsed the leader of the centrist Yashar party to begin coalition talks, after the Arab-dominated Joint List also threw its support behind him, Israeli media reported.
However, that does not guarantee that Eisenkot, the biggest challenger to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, will be successful in forming a government.
He would likely need the backing of both the Joint List and the separate Ra'am party, which together won 19 seats in last month's election, nearly doubling their previous representation and giving them considerable influence over the formation of the next government.
Finding agreement to achieve a majority could prove a struggle as two of Eisenkot's allies have previously ruled out cooperation with Arab parties.
Israel's political future remains uncertain following the parliamentary elections on October 27 that gave neither of the main blocs - Netanyahu's right-wing camp and Eisenkot's centrist alliance - a majority.
Netanyahu's Likud party won the most seats in the 120-member Knesset, securing 27, followed by Eisenkot's Yashar party with 21.
President Herzog has been holding talks with party representatives since Wednesday evening, with each party given the opportunity to recommend a candidate to be tasked with forming a government.
He is scheduled to meet with representatives from Likud and Yashar on Thursday evening, after which the president will determine the candidate he believes has the best chance of securing a parliamentary majority.
The person does not need to be the leader of the largest party, with Eisenkot expected to be given the first shot after the strong backing he received.
The Joint List said backing Eisenkot had been a difficult decision, in a statement cited by Israeli media.
"Although we are determined to oust Netanyahu, the opposition camp led by Eisenkot has so far failed to show the necessary willingness to engage with Netanyahu's policies and to combat the incitement against Arab citizens," the alliance was quoted as saying by the ynet news site.
Netanyahu's Likud accused the Arab parties of electoral fraud, allegations that have since been rejected by the police and the electoral authority.
In his first video message released since the election on Wednesday evening, Netanyahu again railed against the Arab parties, warning against a government "that is dependent on extremist Islam and Islamist parties."
Netanyahu, who is Israel's longest-serving prime minister, is seeking a seventh term.

articles.title_orig: Motorola is going ultra premium with its $1,600 ‘Signature’ phone
articles.title_zh: Motorola is going ultra premium with its $1,600 ‘Signature’ phone
articles.content_orig:
Motorola is patching a hole in its US lineup with a non-folding flagship phone, but the pricing puts this device dangerously close to the company’s expensive tablet-style foldable . The long-rumored Motorola Signature 27 is real, featuring top-of-the-line specs, a super-bright OLED screen, and a ton of cameras. But all this high-end hardware won’t come cheap in the age of AI. Motorola’s new flagship smartphone will run a whopping $1,600 when it arrives later this month.
The Signature 27 is a completely new take on flagship smartphones from Motorola, leaving behind the middling legacy of the Edge series. However, you’ll still immediately clock this as a Motorola device due to its distinctive use of materials and Pantone colors. The phone is metal, ceramic, and glass, but the backs are textured polycarbonate. The device comes in Coal Smoke (black) or Capulet Olive (green) colors. The former has a “tactical weave” finish inspired by automotive design, and the latter is “textile-inspired.”
This device will include the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, the most powerful mobile chip Qualcomm offers right now. While some smartphones have flirted with 16GB of memory, that’s less common these days. The Signature 27 will have 12GB like Samsung’s base model flagships. However, there’s not going to be an upgrade option for more. You will, however, get a generous 512GB of storage.
The phone is fairly thin in most places, but it tapers outward near the camera module. It’s easy to see why Moto needed a little more space up there with four image sensors. Note: That’s not four cameras . There are three standard cameras: a 50MP primary, a 50MP ultrawide, and a 200MP 3x optical zoom (100x digital zoom). Joining the cameras is an event-based vision sensor (EVS) to power a feature called Action Shot.
The action sensor measures changes in light at a pixel level, which makes it ideal for tracking moving subjects. Action Shot will turn on automatically when the phone detects a lot of movement in the frame, but you can also activate it manually. Motorola’s cameras have long struggled to capture moving subjects clearly, so it’ll be interesting to see if the EVS fixes that.
If you’ve been thinking about a smaller phone, the Signature 27 isn’t for you. This phone sports a sizable 6.8-inch OLED screen with a 120Hz refresh rate. This is a tandem OLED panel, which uses stacked pixels to increase brightness. Moto claims the Signature 27 can hit an impressive 12,000 nits of peak brightness, which is four times higher than the iPhone 18 Pro Max (and the highest of any smartphone). A possible drawback is that tandem OLEDs tend to have a somewhat uneven appearance at low brightness with solid colors, but we haven’t seen the Signature 27 in person yet to say whether or not that’s the case here.
A display like that could really drain your battery, but the Signature 27 has capacity to spare. The 7,000 mAh silicon-carbon cell is the largest of any mainstream smartphone, 1,000 mAh larger than the Galaxy S26 Ultra . Motorola estimates it could last two days on a charge, and it won’t take long to refill. With a compatible USB-C charger (not included), the Signature 27 can reach speeds up to 90W. Moto claims up to 12 hours of usage in 12 minutes of charging.
The Motorola Signature 27 will ship with Android 17 and Moto’s Hello UI customizations. The company promises seven years of OS updates, on par with Samsung and Google.
This will be a full Gemini Intelligence device, entitling it to Google’s most expansive list of AI features. Moto says the Signature 27 will get Google’s agentic app control, Create My Widget, Sign-to-Text, and Rambler voice input. However, these features will arrive “in the coming months,” as most of those features are still limited to Pixel phones.
Moto is still offering a parallel set of AI features on its phones. Features like Catch me up (notification summaries) and Pay Attention (meeting notes) are still supported, but the company appears to have dropped the Moto AI branding. Instead, these are all part of Motorola Qira, an AI platform that also connects your Motorola phone to Lenovo computers.
But what if you don’t want any of that? The Motorola Signature 27 will offer an uncharacteristic level of choice. This is the first Moto phone covered under its partnership with GrapheneOS. This privacy-focused OS is built on Android, but it doesn’t have Google apps or any of the tracking that comes with it.
Credit:
                                      Motorola Credit:

          
          Motorola
Motorola does not intend to ship a version of the Signature 27 with GrapheneOS preloaded, so it’ll be up to buyers to install it. Details on that process will come at a later date, but it should be similar to Pixel phones—unlock the bootloader, flash the software, and enjoy.
Some months back, the Graphene team revealed the first device in its Moto collaboration would be priced above Pixels , and that certainly checks out. Motorola is asking $1,599.99 for the Signature 27, putting it above even the high-end flagship phones from Samsung and Apple. It’s also within $300 dollars of foldable phones like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Motorola’s own Razr Fold (both $1,900 MSRP). Even the iPhone Duo is only $400 more than Moto’s new flagship slab.
Moto hasn’t announced any carrier partnerships yet. So you’ll have to buy the device directly from Motorola, Best Buy, or Amazon when it goes on sale November 26. Preorders will be available starting November 19 if you are so inclined.

articles.title_orig: World of Warcraft: Forever has gone live, and players are calling it the smoothest launch in WoW history
articles.title_zh: World of Warcraft: Forever has gone live, and players are calling it the smoothest launch in WoW history
articles.content_orig:
Editor's Note: This initial review-in-progress is based entirely on time spent in the pre-release beta, and will be updated as we get deeper into into the full game.
I was there, Gandalf. I was there when the World of Warcraft opened its servers for the first time in 2004 – which might not literally be 10,000 years ago, but sometimes it feels like it. And now that I've put a good 30 hours into the beta for World of Warcraft: Forever, I'm looking forward to today's launch in a way I haven't for almost any game in a long time. GTA 6 can wait.
It may surprise you to hear me say that and then follow it up with the fact that I had essentially zero interest in World of Warcraft: Classic back in 2019. In fact, I wrote one of my favorite articles ever about exactly why that was. But Forever is different. It's built on the bones of Classic, but with just the right amount of modern sensibilities baked in. There are new zones to discover, much-needed class changes, and some truly impressive graphical enhancements. So, I invite you to come on this journey with me, as it's going to be a bit different from our typical game reviews.
The thing is, Forever is made to be savored. I almost didn't want to review it at all, given how deadline pressure can sometimes warp the experience of something this big. Blizzard really wants this new take on their storied MMO to be about the journey, not the destination – and we plan to honor that here. This will be more of a long-form critique that's going to hearken back to an old Blizzard motto from their golden age: It will be done when it's done. Anything less wouldn't be a review of World of Warcraft: Forever so much as a review of rushing through World of Warcraft: Forever in a stressful and unintended way.
As such, I plan to update this piece as I climb my way to level 60 and discover all the new things there are to discover at the sort of pace I think would make sense if I didn't have a hard deadline. I still expect to have some kind of a firmer verdict before everyone wanders off for the December holidays. But if you want to know whether I think it's worth jumping in right now, on launch day, I can start by sharing my impressions from the beta.
As an avid player of Modern WoW until very recently, and someone who skipped Classic altogether, it's almost a revelation to open up my character sheet in Forever and see 23 years of what I can only describe as "streamlinesh**tification" stripped away. Like, dang, this used to be so much more of an RPG! All the modern game's stat pruning, summary execution of mechanics that added character but were demonized as "inconvenient," class role homogenization, and so much more added up to a death by thousands of cuts that you almost wouldn't notice if you stayed subscribed from the beginning because it was generally so gradual.I love having features like parry, block, and hit chance back. I love leveling up my different weapon skills when I hit a new level. I love that we have more secondary stats to worry about than just crit, haste, versatility, and mastery. I even love having to go buy my skill ranks every level, because it makes me learn where the hub for my class is in each major city and meet the key NPCs I can hang with and look up to. I love that levelling actually takes a long time. This was important stuff that was slashed to try and create a frictionless slope that would never alienate anyone ever, and the modern game is much poorer for having lost it.
Azeroth is so much more interesting to explore on foot, too. Flying mounts are fun, especially with the post-Dragonflight skyriding system. (They are!) But zooming around through the air as the default mode of travel has taken so much of the character of exploration and discovery out of Modern. Forever insisting that you spend the first 40 levels without even the speed boost of a ground mount allowed me to reconnect with this world in ways that really made me feel 14 again. It feels big and dangerous and mysterious. It's wonderful.
And at this point, Forever's new lighting and post-processing make it look better than Modern to me. Yes, I do play with HD models. Sorry to all the SD purists, but I don't think the player races in particular actually hold up visually in 2026. I'm glad we can both pick the graphics we prefer. But regardless, these zones look stunning. They did go overboard with the fog in some areas, I think. But overall, I love the enhancements and going back to Modern feels like a straight downgrade.
I do have some concerns already. One of them is the "realmless" structure, which I think is particularly bad for roleplayers like me. We fought against capital cities having phasing in Modern for a good reason. Splitting up these hubs where people go to find RP tends to do the opposite of building strong communities. Blizzard has been swearing up and down that this is good for the long-term health of Forever. I am completely unconvinced so far, but willing to at least give it a chance.
It's hard to say too much more than that at this point. I ended my beta journey at level 13, gazing out across the dusty plains of Westfall, because I didn't want to spoil too much for myself before the big day. But from what I have seen so far? I think they might have done it. They made me believe I can go home again – and that home is somewhere I want to spend more time, with new surprises to discover. Let's see if they can keep it up for 47 more levels. Watch this space for updates in the weeks to come.

articles.content_orig:
Motorola is officially back in the flagship space, with its new Signature 27 phone available for pre-order starting today, but it’ll cost a pretty penny.
Motorola Signature 27 is, in every sense of the word, a true and proper flagship smartphone, with specs that are more or less unmatched in the US and hold up even in international markets.
The full specs on Motorola Signature 27 include:
Add it all up, this is a true flagship like we’ve never really seen from Motorola, especially in the US.
Motorola also touts that Signature 27 is compatible with GrapheneOS, has an “ArcticMesh” vapor chamber cooling system with diamond-infused thermal gel, and reiterates just how bright that display is. The Tandem OLED technology in use is also mentioned to be 34% more energy efficient and have a 121% longer lifespan compared to traditional OLED panels. The speakers are also tuned by Bang & Olufsen, a name we’ve not seen in the Android space since LG was still in the game.
On the software side, Android 17 is available out of the box with the promise of 7 years of OS upgrades and security updates – no promises on how often those will be delivered, though. Motorola is also the first brand outside of Pixel to fully embrace Gemini Intelligence, with Gboard Rambler, “Create My Widget,” app automation, and Sign-To-Text ASL translation all supported on Signature 27.
Battery life should be excellent with a 7,000 mAh cell inside that Motorola says charges at 90W (wired) and uses silicon-carbon battery tech. Wireless charging speeds top out at 50W on Motorola’s charger and it sounds like it maxes out at 15W on other devices based on the company’s communication with us. There appears to be no Qi2 support either, sadly, even though Motorola supports the tech elsewhere in its lineup .
The cameras are not holding back either. The 50MP main shooter uses a Sony Lytia L910 sensor with LOFIC for improved color, brightness, and video, with two other 50MP sensors for the ultrawide and front-facing cameras. There’s also a 200MP periscope telephoto camera that’s only 3x optical quality, but goes all the way to 100x hybrid zoom. Motorola has also equipped the device with a dedicated EVS action sensor that is specifically used to improve clarity and sharpness on fast-moving objects while using an “Action Shot” mode.
Truly, a full flagship across the board, but oh boy it is not cheap.
Motorola Signature 27 is launching in the US for $1,599 on November 19 , with pre-orders open today. That’s for the 512GB/12GB variant that’s also the only one coming to the US, with colors including “Coal Smoke” and “Capulet Olive.” There’s no availability coming to Canada at this time, but US buyers can get a free Moto Watch Ultra (the one with Wear OS) with their pre-order from Motorola.com for a “limited time.” That same offer also includes a free year of the “motocare” extended warranty. There’s no word of carrier launches yet, but Motorola says US units are “universally unlocked.”
What do you think of Motorola Signature 27, and would you pay $1,599 for it?
